Now, regarding the second part of your question, a step function f / [a, b] -> \mathbb{R} is Riemann Integrable. This is a well-known result in real analysis, and the proof is as follows:

Let f be a step function on [a, b]. Then f can be written as a finite linear combination of characteristic functions of intervals:

f(x) = ∑_{i=1}^n c_i \chi_{I_i}(x)

where I_i are disjoint intervals and c_i are constants.

For each interval I_i, we can define a partition P_i of I_i as follows:

P_i = {x_0, x_1,..., x_k}

where x_0 = a and x_k = b.

Then, we can define a Riemann sum for f on the partition P:

S(P) = ∑_{i=1}^n c_i \sum_{j=1}^k f(x_j) \Delta x_j

where \Delta x_j = x_j - x_{j-1}.

Since f is a step function, we have that f(x_j) = c_i for all x_j in I_i.

Therefore, we can rewrite the Riemann sum as:

S(P) = ∑_{i=1}^n c_i \sum_{j=1}^k c_i \Delta x_j

= ∑_{i=1}^n c_i^2 \sum_{j=1}^k \Delta x_j

= ∑_{i=1}^n c_i^2 (b-a)

Since the sum is finite, we can take the limit as the partition P approaches the uniform partition P*, and we get:

∫_a^b f(x) dx = lim_{|P|→0} S(P) = ∑_{i=1}^n c_i^2 (b-a)

Therefore, f is Riemann Integrable, and the integral is equal to the sum of the squares of the coefficients times the length of the interval.

Note that this proof assumes that the step function f is defined on the closed interval [a, b], and that the partition P is a uniform partition of the interval. If the step function is defined on an open interval, the proof is similar, but the partition P must be a uniform partition of the open interval.
